related_questions.question: Can non-US citizens get a Social Security number?

text_blocks.snippet: Yes, non-US citizens can get a Social Security number, but it's not automatic. Generally, non-citizens need permission from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to work in the U.S. to be eligible for an SSN. However, some non-citizens who don't have work authorization from DHS may still need an SSN for other reasons, such as receiving certain non-work related government benefits.

list.snippet: Lawful Permanent Residents: Those with a "green card" are generally eligible for an SSN.
Non-citizens authorized to work by DHS: This includes individuals with work permits (EADs), certain nonimmigrant statuses, asylees, and refugees.

Non-citizens with a valid non-work reason: Some individuals may need an SSN for reasons other than employment, such as for certain government benefits. In these cases, the Social Security Administration (SSA) will issue an SSN with a "NOT VALID FOR EMPLOYMENT" restriction.

list.title: 1. Determine if you need an SSN:
list.snippet: You can check with the Social Security Administration (SSA) or the agency requiring the SSN to see if you need one.

list.title: 2. Gather required documents:
list.snippet: This includes proof of your identity, age, and immigration status. You'll need your original immigration documents (like Form I-94, I-551, or I-766) and potentially other documents depending on your situation.

list.title: 3. Apply for an SSN:
list.snippet: You can apply online and then go to a Social Security office to submit your documents.

list.title: 4. Wait for your card:
list.snippet: The SSA will mail you a Social Security card with your number on it once your application is approved and documents are verified.
An SSN does not grant permission to work or live in the U.S.: It simply means you are part of the Social Security system.
Non-citizens authorized to work by DHS will have an SSN card with the restriction "VALID FOR WORK ONLY WITH DHS AUTHORIZATION", according to the Social Security Administration.
If you have a non-work SSN, you cannot use it to work. Doing so could result in the SSA informing DHS, according to the Social Security Administration.
